newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US pushes for vote on Iraq after Russia compromise.
newsitem.headline: US pushes for vote on Iraq after Russia compromise.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council was expected to vote on Saturday to condemn Iraq for blocking U.N. arms inspectors and threaten further sanctions if Baghdad does not comply, diplomats said.

The new draft resolution was weaker than the United States and Britain wanted. They proposed an immediate travel ban on Iraqi civilian and military officials. But France, China and Egypt had reservations and Russia threatened a veto.

A senior U.S. official said the new compromise text avoided a veto and "accepts the principle of new sanctions." It was forged after President Bill Clinton spoke to Russian President Boris Yeltsin at the Group of Seven industrial nations currently underway in Denver.
Their conversation was followed up by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright speaking to Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and French Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine.
Albright, fluent in both French and Russian, did the translating, the official told Reuters by telephone from Denver, adding that she kept "switching from Russian to French to English."

Iraq in the past month has barred arms inspectors, searching for weapons of mass destruction, from three sensitive sites in what some believe is a change of policy towards the Security Council's mandates.

Baghdad has been under sanctions since its troops invaded Kuwait in August 1990. One condition for lifting sanctions on oil exports is to scrap its weapons of mass destruction and related documents. The council maintains U.N. inspectors are to have free access to suspected sites.

The new draft resolution under consideration by the council, "expresses the firm intention to impose additional measures on those categories on Iraqi officials responsible for the non-compliance." It also suspends regular reviews of sanctions until October.

The resolution needs nine votes for adoption in the 15-seat council and no veto from one of its permanent members -- the United States, France, Britain, Russia and China. On the original U.S.-British draft, Russia had threatened to use its veto while China and France would have abstained.
The new text is expected to be approved by all except China, which will probably still abstain.
Over the past year the council has been split on strong action against Iraq, with the United States losing ground among members of the original coalition that drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait in 1991.

The council last Friday issued a relatively mild statement deploring a series of incidents in which U.N. inspectors said Iraqis had endangered U.N. helicopters and their crews assisting U.N. ground teams. Since then inspectors have been turned away from three sites they attempted to visit.
Chief U.N. arms inspector Rolf Ekeus said last week asked the council to take a firm stand.

"If Iraq is allowed now to decide what we should inspect, when we should inspect it, I think the value of the whole mechanism set up after the Gulf War would be put into question," he said, referring to the U.N. special commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping dangerous Iraqi armaments.

Ekeus, who will leave UNSCOM on July 1 and will be succeeded by Australian U.N. envoy Richard Butler, speculated it "may be because we are changing leadership that Iraq is now trying to change the ground rules somewhat."

Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz, in a letter to the council, said access to some sites had been denied recently because of concern the inspections were not to carry out UNSCOM's mandate but to "detect the arrangements made for the security of Iraq, its leadership and the personnel involved."

Aziz said the UNSCOM team was allowed to inspect 40 out of the 43 sites to which it sought access. Denial of access to the other sites "cannot be interpreted as a decision by the government of Iraq to prevent the special commission implementing its mandate, as Mr. Ekeus alleges," he added.
